hn.originalTitle: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
hn.sourceOriginalText:
AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software - Ars Technica

Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code . But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code , meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output.

A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.”

Cut once, measure twice

To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish , which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026.

To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations.

In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those .

The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write.

In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms.

While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work.

AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. Th

hn.originalTitle: Launch HN: Agent37 (YC F26) – Low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 ( https://agent37.com ). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox. You can view a video walkthrough of the product here: https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses. One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings. Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month. Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost: * When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost. * Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This a.

Comment 1: I had ran into another yc startup from the same batch doing the same thing recently. I think it was called maritime. YC batch are becoming more like hunger games. I know a few companies where this is just a feature like digitalocean it is just a feature.

Comment 2: I'd be curious to see stats on overlap among startups by batch historically. My impression is that this has always been a thing. Based on where the market/technology horizon currently is, there are some buckets that are very "startup shaped". Founders who are iterating on ideas using similar criteria will often end up in the same proximity, especially in an accelerator environment. But it would be extremely interesting to see if this has become more prevalent over time, or at least since the explosion in the AI market.

Comment 3: It is also funny to see folks and friends of the startup commenting and trying to boost this post which is against the guidelines, but thats ok.

Comment 4: Yeah its a race to the bottom as ai can vibe code any infra now

hn.originalTitle: A look at OpenAI’s math that’s claimed computes faster Fourier transforms
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Faster Fourier Transforms - by Ben Recht - arg min

Faster Fourier Transforms

The OpenAI algorithm for the FFT is less a breakthrough and more a malicious exploit.

Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post looks at part of OpenAI’s math repository that claims to compute faster Fourier transforms. It’s more technical than usual, but I tried to add some tutorial material for people who need a refresher course on signal processing or computational complexity.

The Fast Fourier Transform is one of the most important innovations in digital signal processing and one of my favorite algorithms. The FFT is a fast way to extract the frequency content of signals, letting you rapidly analyze, filter, and manipulate frequencies across different bands of the spectrum.

The Fourier transform computes the energy in each frequency band through a simple dot product. 1 Let x denote your input, a length n array of samples, and f a frequency. Then the amount of frequency content in x at f can be computed by the formula:

For digital signals, a bit of math shows you only need to compute n of these dot products, one at each multiple of the frequency 2𝜋/n, to understand all of the frequency content. Naively, this requires n multiplications and additions for each frequency. Hence, computing the entire Fourier transform appears to require n 2 arithmetic operations.

The fast Fourier transform is a clever recursive procedure devised by James Cooley and John Tukey in 1965. 2 The main idea is that a length-n Fourier transform can be computed by shuffling the input vector, computing two Fourier transforms of length n/2 on the shuffled components, and then recombining the outputs using atomic arithmetic operations. The shuffles and recombinations take a linear number of arithmetic operations. Repeating this procedure iteratively, namely, log 2 (n) times, computes the full discrete Fourier transform. With the bookkeeping, the FFT computes a length-n Fourier transform in fewer than 5 n log2 n arithmetic operations.

To make this acceleration concrete, when n is 1,000, n^2 is 1,000,000 and 5 * n log n is around 50,000, a 20-fold speedup. When n is 1,000,000, the speedup is 10,000-fold. These speedups can be the difference between a transform being computable or not given the constraints of a signal processing application.

Since the invention of the FFT, people have looked for even faster Fourier transforms. One question is just how fast you can go. It seems like you probably need at least n operations to compute the FFT, as it takes n steps just to write it down. The FFT is 5*log 2 (n) times slower than that reasonable speed limit, and that 5*log 2 (n) factor can be big. It’s 200 when n is a trillion. Can you do something clever to reduce that prefactor of 200?

Well, lo and behold, in the massive paper dump OpenAI took on the mathematics world last week, they claim to have a faster Fourier transform. The main claim from their discriminatively named “main.pdf” is

I was intrigued about what was going on here. The log(n) term, in theory, was a teeny tiny bit smaller than in the standard FFT.

Did I read this paper? Of course not. No one at OpenAI read this paper either, so why should I? I did what every other mathematician in the world does with AI slop mathematics: I fed it back into the slop machine and ran an information retrieval session with a chatbot interface to extract salient facts. Anthropomorphically speaking: I asked ChatGPT what it thinks about its own output. This is how we do mathematical research now. What a world.

Unfortunately, I did not find a faster Fourier transform. Instead,l I found the rot that develops inside applied mathematical theory when formalism becomes so detached from reality that a “breakthrough” is nothing more than an artifact of mathematicians not being able to properly specify the rules of their games in natural language.

First, “big-O” notation has been so abused that it has become meaningless. Let’s review the definition, which impressed me as an undergrad. An algorithm has running time T(n) = O(F(n)) if there exists an integer N and a constant C such that

That is, the number of steps the algorithm actually takes is upper bounded by a constant times some convenient function F(n) as long as n is large. F(n) is usually something familiar and interpretable, like a polynomial or exponential function. This notation says that we only care about what happens when the size of the computation is large. We care about the asymptotic growth rate of the computation time.

hn.originalTitle: "Just Ask Claude" Is a Rare and Valuable Skill
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Comment 1: If I ask you a question and you turn around and ask AI you get to replace me with AI for all future interactions.

Comment 2: If you ask me to "check what AI says", I will ask you to do it yourself and to kindly replace me with your AI for all future interactions.

Comment 3: Hasn't the same always applied to googling on behalf of others? That's why LMGTFY exists too...

Comment 4: It even updated to let you choose the search engine. Surprisingly they haven't updated it to include OpenAI/Claude/Copilot/... guess he should've named the domain "lmFtfy" (s/Google/find/g)

hn.originalTitle: Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks \ Anthropic

Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks

In recent months, we’ve made substantial progress on reducing the effectiveness of distillation attacks on Claude using new methods, as we outline in this blog. Early evidence suggests that these methods have reduced the amount of data harvested by distillers by around 90 to 99 percent.

Distillation attacks are covert, industrial-scale campaigns to extract the capabilities of one model and replicate them in another, without the authorization of the original model’s developers. They are often conducted using networks of fraudulent accounts. These attacks allow companies to mimic frontier capabilities for a fraction of the development time and cost. As we wrote in September , this method has been used extensively to help overseas AI laboratories keep pace with US companies.

We’re concerned about illicit distillation for two reasons. First, distillation enables companies to build models that approach the capability frontier, but which have, in practice, been released without proportionally robust safeguards. This means that distilled models could be used to cause significant harm in areas like biology and cybersecurity .

Zhipu, for example , distilled the cyber capabilities of leading US models during the development of GLM-5.3. The company tried to distill Claude Fable 5—although, after finding that our cyber safeguards degraded its attacks, it switched to an older Claude model and another lab’s model. The US Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) has since assessed GLM-5.3 to be the most cyber-capable open-weights model released to date. Our own research has found that GLM-5.3’s safeguards can easily be bypassed, and that the model is willing to develop security exploits from end-to-end.

Second, illicitly distilled models present a national security risk. The companies that distill US models are integrating the capabilities they gain from distillation into foreign military, intelligence, and surveillance systems . For example, we recently reported on a case in which requests to Moonshot’s Kimi models were secretly forwarded to Claude as part of its distillation efforts. One request came from a user (who we believe was affiliated with China’s People’s Liberation Army) who sought to analyze CCTV surveillance of a specific individual. These are the kinds of capabilities distillers are hoping to develop.

In response to the increasing sophistication and scale of these attacks, we’ve expanded and greatly strengthened our defenses against them. As we’ll describe below, these measures have been successful—although they do involve trade-offs for both Anthropic and our customers. We’ve turned away meaningful revenue and trillions of tokens’ worth of paying traffic from distillers, and our research and product teams have invested substantial time and effort into this problem. Some of our changes have also required legitimate users to make updates to their integrations.

Distillation is a problem that every model developer faces and must confront. We hope this post helps developers and platforms better understand how they can prevent these attacks, what the trade-offs with these measures might be, and why the costs are worth bearing.

Simple defenses are not enough

Distillers aim to generate millions of responses from a larger, more capable model (in this case, Claude), then use those responses to teach a smaller model to mimic the more capable model’s behavior. The most valuable kind of data for this purpose are transcripts of Claude’s reasoning—the thinking process that Claude writes out before it responds. This is much more useful than its output alone, since it helps the smaller model understand how Claude reaches its final answer. Our defenses against distillation therefore focus almost entirely on making Claude’s reasoning harder for distillers to access.

Our early work to combat distillation started with simple measures designed to block passive distillation, in which attackers send requests to the model as a normal user would, and then train on those responses. As one of our initial anti-distillation measures, we had Claude summarize its reasoning before we showed it to users. Our evaluations showed that this made Claude’s transcripts much less informative for distillers. We tested how well a pretrained Claude model performed on the SWE-bench Verified coding benchmark after it was trained on transcripts from Claude Opus

This is much more useful than its output alone, since it helps the smaller model understand how Claude reaches its final answer. Our defenses against distillation therefore focus almost entirely on making Claude’s reasoning harder for distillers to access.

Our early work to combat distillation started with simple measures designed to block passive distillation, in which attackers send requests to the model as a normal user would, and then train on those responses. As one of our initial anti-distillation measures, we had Claude summarize its reasoning before we showed it to users. Our evaluations showed that this made Claude’s transcripts much less informative for distillers. We tested how well a pretrained Claude model performed on the SWE-bench Verified coding benchmark after it was trained on transcripts from Claude Opus

hn.originalTitle: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
hn.sourceOriginalText:
AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software - Ars Technica

Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code . But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code , meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output.

A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.”

Cut once, measure twice

To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish , which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026.

To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations.

In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those .

The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write.

In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms.

While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work.

AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. Th

hn.originalTitle: Launch HN: Agent37 (YC F26) – Low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 ( https://agent37.com ). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox. You can view a video walkthrough of the product here: https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses. One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings. Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month. Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost: * When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost. * Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This a.

Comment 1: I had ran into another yc startup from the same batch doing the same thing recently. I think it was called maritime. YC batch are becoming more like hunger games. I know a few companies where this is just a feature like digitalocean it is just a feature.

Comment 2: I'd be curious to see stats on overlap among startups by batch historically. My impression is that this has always been a thing. Based on where the market/technology horizon currently is, there are some buckets that are very "startup shaped". Founders who are iterating on ideas using similar criteria will often end up in the same proximity, especially in an accelerator environment. But it would be extremely interesting to see if this has become more prevalent over time, or at least since the explosion in the AI market.

Comment 3: It is also funny to see folks and friends of the startup commenting and trying to boost this post which is against the guidelines, but thats ok.

Comment 4: Yeah its a race to the bottom as ai can vibe code any infra now

hn.originalTitle: A look at OpenAI’s math that’s claimed computes faster Fourier transforms
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Faster Fourier Transforms - by Ben Recht - arg min

Faster Fourier Transforms

The OpenAI algorithm for the FFT is less a breakthrough and more a malicious exploit.

Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post looks at part of OpenAI’s math repository that claims to compute faster Fourier transforms. It’s more technical than usual, but I tried to add some tutorial material for people who need a refresher course on signal processing or computational complexity.

The Fast Fourier Transform is one of the most important innovations in digital signal processing and one of my favorite algorithms. The FFT is a fast way to extract the frequency content of signals, letting you rapidly analyze, filter, and manipulate frequencies across different bands of the spectrum.

The Fourier transform computes the energy in each frequency band through a simple dot product. 1 Let x denote your input, a length n array of samples, and f a frequency. Then the amount of frequency content in x at f can be computed by the formula:

For digital signals, a bit of math shows you only need to compute n of these dot products, one at each multiple of the frequency 2𝜋/n, to understand all of the frequency content. Naively, this requires n multiplications and additions for each frequency. Hence, computing the entire Fourier transform appears to require n 2 arithmetic operations.

The fast Fourier transform is a clever recursive procedure devised by James Cooley and John Tukey in 1965. 2 The main idea is that a length-n Fourier transform can be computed by shuffling the input vector, computing two Fourier transforms of length n/2 on the shuffled components, and then recombining the outputs using atomic arithmetic operations. The shuffles and recombinations take a linear number of arithmetic operations. Repeating this procedure iteratively, namely, log 2 (n) times, computes the full discrete Fourier transform. With the bookkeeping, the FFT computes a length-n Fourier transform in fewer than 5 n log2 n arithmetic operations.

To make this acceleration concrete, when n is 1,000, n^2 is 1,000,000 and 5 * n log n is around 50,000, a 20-fold speedup. When n is 1,000,000, the speedup is 10,000-fold. These speedups can be the difference between a transform being computable or not given the constraints of a signal processing application.

Since the invention of the FFT, people have looked for even faster Fourier transforms. One question is just how fast you can go. It seems like you probably need at least n operations to compute the FFT, as it takes n steps just to write it down. The FFT is 5*log 2 (n) times slower than that reasonable speed limit, and that 5*log 2 (n) factor can be big. It’s 200 when n is a trillion. Can you do something clever to reduce that prefactor of 200?

Well, lo and behold, in the massive paper dump OpenAI took on the mathematics world last week, they claim to have a faster Fourier transform. The main claim from their discriminatively named “main.pdf” is

I was intrigued about what was going on here. The log(n) term, in theory, was a teeny tiny bit smaller than in the standard FFT.

Did I read this paper? Of course not. No one at OpenAI read this paper either, so why should I? I did what every other mathematician in the world does with AI slop mathematics: I fed it back into the slop machine and ran an information retrieval session with a chatbot interface to extract salient facts. Anthropomorphically speaking: I asked ChatGPT what it thinks about its own output. This is how we do mathematical research now. What a world.

Unfortunately, I did not find a faster Fourier transform. Instead,l I found the rot that develops inside applied mathematical theory when formalism becomes so detached from reality that a “breakthrough” is nothing more than an artifact of mathematicians not being able to properly specify the rules of their games in natural language.

First, “big-O” notation has been so abused that it has become meaningless. Let’s review the definition, which impressed me as an undergrad. An algorithm has running time T(n) = O(F(n)) if there exists an integer N and a constant C such that

That is, the number of steps the algorithm actually takes is upper bounded by a constant times some convenient function F(n) as long as n is large. F(n) is usually something familiar and interpretable, like a polynomial or exponential function. This notation says that we only care about what happens when the size of the computation is large. We care about the asymptotic growth rate of the computation time.

There's little that's "inevitable" about AI | deadSimpleTech

Get new articles delivered to your inbox → Enter your email Enter your email Get Updates → Also send me the monthly newsletter There's little that's "inevitable" about AI Author: Iris Meredith Date published: 2026-10-10 About as common as the statement that AI technology is just a tool is the statement that AI is "inevitable", so we should all just give up and get with the program because the technology is definitely going to persist and we're definitely going to give up our thinking to the machines. This is obviously a thought-terminating cliche, but it's work digging into a little further: after all, given how much it's being said, it would be worth knowing exactly how and why it's wrong..

The task in question is socially valuable: we need a lot of it done, and it's currently done by labour that is, in some sense, scarce

The technology can, in volume of adequate output or in quality of output, overwhelmingly outclass what alternative technologies can do. A moderate improvement isn't really enough to force inevitability: it has to be a massive difference.

There's no way in which the people not using the technology can change their behaviour to neutralise the impact of the technology. Firearms were overwhelming in this sense while the counterweight trebuchet wasn't because, while it's essentially impossible to mitigate the impact of cannon without radical changes to how fortifications are built, a counterweight trebuchet can have its impact blunted with incremental changes.

Unless all of these conditions hold, the adoption of a given technology can be fairly held to be contingent and not inevitable: it's not a choice that a social grouping was forced into, but one that they chose relatively freely. In short, inevitable technologies are ones where, if you don't adopt them, you will swiftly be overwhelmed by the cultures and societies that do. This seems to me to be largely in keeping with the way that LLM advocates use the term: LLM technology is inevitable because people who don't use it will fall so far behind those that do in power that they will end up under the control of LLM users.

Looking at this, we can quite clearly see the pattern of inevitability when it comes to gunpowder. A cannon can breach a curtain wall much faster than a counterweight trebuchet, and more efficiently too. Breaching curtain walls is something that, in a fragmented mediaeval Europe, is very socially valuable: if you can breach a wall, you can take a city or a castle, and the faster you do that, the less time you have to spend laying siege. Cannon is overwhelmingly more powerful than other kinds of siege equipment, and even early small arms were able to deliver overwhelmingly more energy in a shot than an equivalent crossbow or longbow could. Finally, there wasn't any particularly easy way to n.

We might compare this, for purposes of discussion, against the magnetic compass. The magnetic compass meets the first two criteria: it works a hell of a lot better for finding north than taking sightings of the sun and calculating does, and it works even absent known landmarks. Moreover, knowing the direction of north is rather useful when you're a maritime power and want to be able to navigate effectively. However, it's not overwhelmingly efficient: you can still navigate effectively without one, and it's easy enough to neutralise simply by virtue of not taking an interest in maritime activities and becoming a land power . Thus, while the magnetic compass allowed the colonial powers of Eur.

Are modern LLMs inevitable?

So how does modern AI (in the LLM sense) measure up against these standards?

The first point is the question of whether an LLM can do work not markedly inferior to that of a human doing the same task or not. This one is debatable. An LLM absolutely cannot produce work to the highest human standards, or even a good human standard at the moment, and it's unlikely that it ever will. Most human work, however, is not done at a good standard. At best it's mediocre, and at worst it's downright horrible. The bulk of human knowledge work done in an awful of settings, then, is unfortunately more or less interchangeable with that of an LLM (seriously, so much human work is just awful: I wish I could say otherwise). On this point, then, LLMs probably pass the criterion.

The next question is that of social value. A lot of the knowledge work that LLMs purport to replace is scarce and valued: the writing of software, research work, graph
